beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: On the way to Jerusalem, Jesus walked the borderland between Samaria and Galilee — the seam between two peoples who despised each other. Keep that seam in mind. It matters at the end of this story.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: As he reached a village, ten men met him — but they stopped far off, strung along a rise, and came no closer. They were lepers. The Law of Moses required them to live outside the town and to warn everyone away. That gap of empty ground between them and the road was not shyness. It was the law. These were ten men no one had touched in years.

beats.text: When he saw them, he did not close the distance. He did not touch them, and he did not announce that they were healed. He simply gave them an instruction:

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: Now, why send them to a priest? Because in Israel the priest was the only inspector who could certify a leper clean and let him back into his family, his work, his worship. Sending them was a promise in disguise. That errand only made sense one way: if they would be clean by the time they arrived.

beats.text: But nothing had changed yet. They looked at each other, at their own still-bandaged hands, at the long road to a city they had no proof they would be welcome in. And then, one by one, they turned and started walking anyway.

card.text: The healing happened while they walked, before they could see it. Have you ever had to move forward on nothing but a word — before there was any proof?
